title: Quant noise source mapping and kernel signature notes
content:
Purpose: map and quantify sources of performance and quality noise introduced by low-precision kernels (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ) and identify action paths for deterministic mitigation and routing policies. This is a field notes-style doc capturing methods, early results, and next steps.

High level hypothesis:
1) "noise" during runs is composed of at least three separable components: kernel-internal numeric sensitivity, memory subsystem jitter (bandwidth & cache collisions), and scheduler-induced micro-interleaving.
2) Different kernels (vectorized fp8 kernels vs packed int8 kernels vs per-layer GPTQ microkernels) exhibit distinct fingerprint patterns in latency distribution and output-regret when stressed with long-context or bursty traffic.
3) If we can attribute % of observed quality/regret variance to each source (numeric vs infra vs scheduling), we can design routing/fallback rules that yield predictable end-to-end SLOs while preserving most of the cost benefit of quantization.

Methodology (how we measured):
- Bench harness: modified traffic-replay tool (local harness + k8s runner) that replays production-like request sequences with preserved inter-arrival times and token distributions. Each experiment run includes an explicit seed for RNG-affecting kernels.
- Models: rw-mid-7b-v3 (baseline float32), rw-large-34b-gptq, rw-large-34b-awq, llama2-70b-int8-pruned (representative long-context behaviour).
- Kernels under test: generic GEMM-packed-INT8, vectorized-FP8-direct, per-layer-GPTQ-microbatch (single-threaded kernel + multithreaded fallback), AWQ-blocked-kernel.
- Metrics: median latency, p95/p99 tail, tokens/sec, Quality-regret (delta in Rouge/BLEU/LL on eval prompts), and a custom metric Noise Contribution Ratio (NCR) described below.
- Instrumentation: Linux perf counters, nvprof-like traces for HW cycles, custom counters for cache-miss patterns, per-kernel wall-time and instruction retirement distribution.
- Repeatability: 10 runs per configuration, each run 30 minutes with warmup 5 minutes; capture per-token timing surface and output tokens to diff against float baseline.

Noise Contribution Ratio (NCR):
- Definition (informal): for each run, partition observed variance in quality/regret and latency into buckets attributable to (A) numeric rounding/deterministic quantization error, (B) kernel-level nondeterminism (e.g., reduction order), (C) memory/cache bandwidth stalls and eviction collisions, (D) scheduler preemption/micro-interleaving.
- Computation approach: use controlled micro-experiments toggling individual factors: run identical RNG-seeded kernel vs alternate kernel, pin threads and isolate CPU affinity, run with kernel-level deterministic-mode (if supported) vs fast path, and compare runs with warmed PV cache vs cold. NCR is percent of variance explained by each toggled factor (ANOVA-esque decomposition over repeated runs).

Selected observations (raw notes):
- Numeric vs infra split: for AWQ-blocked-kernel on rw-large-34b, observed mean quality-regret delta to float was ~1.7% absolute on open-domain eval set. Out of observed sample variance across runs, ~65% was explained by numeric determinism (A+B) while ~35% by infra/scheduling (C+D).
- Kernel fingerprint: vectorized-FP8 kernels produce tight median latency but wider tail (p99 shifted right by ~1.8x) when context > 4k tokens. Root cause signal: periodic cache-thrashing where kernel working set crosses L2 size threshold.
- Packed-INT8 kernels show lower median latency overall but more frequent large spikes during multitenant workloads; spike correlation with bandwidth saturation (PCIe->HBM contention) and concurrent memcpy patterns from kv-cache restoration.
- GPTQ microkernel (single-threaded reduction) is highly stable for short contexts; for >8k contexts, observed increased lock contention on scheduler yielding 20–30% higher p99 on heavy concurrency.

New micro-metrics we used:
- Kernel Signature Fingerprint (KSF): vector of {median kernel-time, p95 kernel-time, cache-miss-rate, %time in memcopy, instruction-branch-entropy}. Used for clustering kernel behaviour under different loads.
- Per-layer jitter map: heatmap of per-layer latency variance vs layer index; useful for spotting layer-localized quant noise or memory bounce.
- Prefix-stability score: measure of how much output distribution drifts when prefixes are identical but execution environment (affinity/placement) differs. High prefix instability implies infra-induced nondeterminism.

Representative numbers (single-run illustrative):
- rw-large-34b-awq, 4 concurrent workers, context 4096: median token latency 18 ms, p95 31 ms, p99 55 ms, quality-regret 1.7% relative. NCR: numeric 43%, kernel-nondet 22%, memory 25%, scheduler 10%.
- rw-large-34b-gptq, 8 workers, context 8192: median 24 ms, p95 48 ms, p99 120 ms (spikes), quality-regret 2.3%. NCR: numeric 52%, kernel-nondet 10%, memory 28%, scheduler 10%.

Root-cause vignettes (repro playbacks):
- Case A: periodic 200–400 ms p99 spikes aligned with a background snapshot job (dev-experiments) that triggered large memcpy of a cached model shard. Mitigation: enforce memcpys to use non-blocking DMA path or schedule snapshot during low-burst windows.
- Case B: lower-quality tail during multi-tenant bursts traced to int8 packing kernel that falls back to scalar reduction for certain layer sizes; fallback path was not vectorized and was single-threaded — fix is to add a parallel path or mask layer shapes for pre-compilation.
- Case C: reproducible drift in beam-ranking scores between two otherwise-identical runs; root cause was differing reduction order in AVX512 codepath for int8 matrix multiply which alters rounding accumulation; we added a deterministic-accumulate mode to the kernel which removed this drift at ~10% perf cost.

Practical routing/fallback rules proposed:
- For latency-sensitive low-burst traffic: prefer packed-INT8 with pinned-thread placement and prewarmed cache; enforce single-tenant allocation on worst-case layer shapes.
- For long-context high-quality routes: prefer FP8 vectorized kernels with adaptive cache warming; route to FP8 when prefix-stability score for the model-instance falls above threshold.
- Canary + NCR gate: when rolling a quant kernel, run canary with controlled replay and require NCR numeric component >= target and infra components <= threshold before auto-rollout.

Engineering actions and TODOs: (owner in parens)
- Add deterministic-accumulate flag to int8 kernels and expose to runtime (Ravi).
- Add Kernel Signature Fingerprint exporter to observability pipeline (Lena).
- Improve traffic-replay harness to emulate memcopy-heavy snapshot jobs in background (Connor).
- Run a 48-hour blocked-run across dedicated hosts to quantify long-tail degradation under mixed workloads (Ava).

Open questions and unresolved tradeoffs:
- What is an acceptable perf hit threshold to enable deterministic accumulation for int8 across all customers? Need product input on revenue vs SLA sensitivity.
- Can we automatically detect and classify memcopy collision patterns in the console and surface advice? (Observability + product work).
- Are there workload features (token entropy, instruction spread) that reliably predict kernel-induced quality degradation? If yes, add model-level routing suggestions in Optimize.

Communication snippets to include in rollout PR:
- Short note for SRE: "When you see p99 spikes coincident with snapshot tasks, consider throttling snapshot DMA or schedule on different nodes; we've added a flag to mark snapshots as low-priority."
- Note for Product: "We can implement an NCR gate on canaries to avoid blind kernel swaps; initial threshold proposals included in linked JIRA."

Appendix (quick commands & references):
- perf wrapper used: ./perf-runner --trace-kernels --pin-cpus --affinity-map conf/affinity-4w.json --seed 3429
- Flamegraph tip: focus on per-token stack rather than cumulative across request to separate warmup vs steady state.

Bottom line summary (short):
- Quant noise is multi-factor. ~40–70% of quality variance is genuine numeric behaviour; the rest is infrastructure and scheduling that we can mitigate without changing quant algorithms. Building NCR-based gating plus a small set of kernel-side determinism knobs lets us safely capture most cost benefits while keeping regression risk bounded.

Filed follow-ups: SRT-4823 (NCR gating), SRT-4831 (deterministic-int8-mode), SRT-4832 (ksf-exporter).

Notes-to-self: capture two more cross-arch runs (A100 vs GH200) to compare NV cache behavior; also test with bursty client patterns that have periodic large prefix resets (these appear to amplify memory-induced spikes).

End of notes.
